text: Each map holds 537 hits. On one, every hit landed by pure chance. The other follows a rule. Which one is chance? Both are simulated, but the question is real. In 1944, Londoners claimed German flying bombs fell in clusters, and precise aim would put factories at risk. Build the detector your eye is running. Cut each map into 576 squares, count the hits, and flag any square with three or more, like this one. Map A lights up with 39 targets. Map B gets none. So A looks aimed, and B looks like chance. Backwards. I dropped every hit on map A at random, so all 39 targets are false alarms. Map B's rule, no two hits closer than 4 fifths of a square. The detector, like your eye, expected chance to spread out that evenly. Take one square. Each bomb has a 1 in 500 and 76 chance of landing in it. To stay empty, all 537 must miss. Guess how many squares get no hit at all? About 200 and 27 squares stay empty. Map A has 222. Those gaps force the clumps. The other 354 squares share all the hits, one and a half each, so plenty must double up. Call the average hits per square lambda. One minus a small slice, raised to a big power, is almost exactly e to the minus lambda. For two hits, pick which two bombs land here. 537 times 536 over two ways. Each lands with chance one in 576 and the rest miss E to the minus lambda again 536 is almost 537 so for any k each two becomes a k the powers merge into lambda to the k, the Poisson distribution. Times 576 squares, it predicts these purple bars. The honest detector compares whole histograms. Map A sits on the purple bars. 39 targets and chance predicts 39. The chi-squared misfit. Square each bar's gap, divide by chance's bar, and add them up. Map A scores 2.0. Pure chance maps score worse three times than four. P equals 0.74. Map B, half the expected empty squares, a tower of single hits, and a misfit of 272. A pattern this even is the fingerprint of a spacing rule. Aimed bombs would miss the other way. Extra empty squares, extra pileups. In 1946, the actuary R.D. Clark published this test on real flying bomb hits. 537 in 576 squares of South London. Chance predicted 227 empty squares. Clark counted 229. Single hits, 211, exactly as predicted. Same test, P equals 0.88. No sign of clustering. That doesn't mean the bombs were un-aimed. They were aimed at London, just too loosely to choose a street. And the test needs one lambda everywhere. Farther north, hits fell about half as densely, so Clark chose an area where lambda held steady. So look again. The clumps in Map A are what no aim at all looks like. If you picked Map B, you pick the one following a rule.
